beats.title: THE TWO SENTENCES
beats.narration_text: Tanmay Kulkarni, for Humanitarians AI. In Mycroft, a public repository, a recipe is a list of steps with a script behind each one. Mine fetches prices for five stocks and adds them up. In the recipe I wrote that step three reads the price files directly, since step two is still open. And that step five reads step three's output, since step four is still open. Those are my sentences, and when I wrote them they were true. Each is a stand-in: a shortcut for a step that did not exist yet. So I will put one check to each. What did it stand in for? What did it skip? And what happens when it and the real step get the same wrong input?

beats.title: THE REAL STEP
beats.narration_text: This week the real step two was merged. It reads the run settings and the workflow, then each price file, and checks every file against the hash recorded in a manifest when the sample files were made. It keeps each file exactly as it came. A file goes to a reject list if the manifest does not list it, if its hash has changed, if it is missing, or if it is not valid jay-son. It does not judge whether a price makes sense. That stays with steps three and four.

beats.title: WHAT THE STAND-IN GOT RIGHT
beats.narration_text: First, the good news. I ran the stand-in and the real step on the same six sets of sample files, and they saw the same files every time. In the clean set, five files and five records. In the set of deliberately defective files, step two took in four and turned one away, while step three looked at the same five and rejected all of them, for its own reasons. Six sets out of six: the shortcut was right about which files were there.

beats.title: THE OLD ROUTE
beats.narration_text: Here is what the old route did. Step one checks the files against the manifest, and it stopped. Its message says: fixture changed since the manifest froze it. But step three, run on the same folder, said pass: five promoted, none rejected. And step five priced the portfolio at sixty-six thousand eight hundred ninety-eight dollars and thirteen cents. The committed run says sixty-five thousand ninety-eight dollars and thirteen cents. That is eighteen hundred dollars more, from two switched digits, and a return of twenty-four point three five percent instead of twenty-one.

beats.title: WHERE THE STOP LIVED
beats.narration_text: I want to be careful here. Step one did stop. What step three, on its own, has no way to know is that it did. Each step is a separate command, and the stop was only a message in a file until someone read it. The stand-in never had to ask the question, because I had put the question somewhere else. Nobody was wrong. It was my sentence, since step two is still open, doing exactly what it said.

beats.narration_text: Now the same folder, through the real step two. Four files taken in. The same wrong file, through a different door, and this time it is stopped by the step whose job is to ask. Wiring step three to read what step two kept is the next change. I have not made it.

beats.title: TWO QUESTIONS
beats.narration_text: So what did the stand-in skip? Two questions. Is this file one that was ever recorded? And is it the same file that was recorded? Step three asked whether a file parsed, named one of my five tickers, and had a price. It never asked whether it was the very file I had recorded. A hash can only say a file is unchanged. It cannot say the file is right. But unchanged was exactly what was missing.

beats.title: WHAT YOURS SKIPPED
beats.narration_text: If you build out of order, you have stand-ins too. Search your own notes for the words since and until. For each one, write down what it replaced and what it skipped. Then, when the real step arrives, hand the stand-in and the real step one deliberately wrong input, and read where they disagree. That one wrong file told me more than six clean sets.

beats.title: WHAT I DID NOT CHECK
beats.narration_text: Here is what I did not check. This was sample mode, with invented prices: one swapped pair, in one file, in one recipe. Step one does catch it when it is run and read; my claim is only about step three on its own. No live call was made. The wrong file was a scratch copy, so none of it is in the repository, and the recipe's own text is unedited, so it still says step two is open.
